stem: Out of all childhood exanthems, what is one infection that you should always remember as a medical emergency? What should you do?
answer: Meningococcemia caused by Neisseria meningitides. When you see fever with petechial/purpuric rash, it’s meningococcemia until proven otherwise. To work up, blood and CSF cultre should be ordered. You should provide timely treatment because it’s associated with high mortality and morbidity including hearing loss, neurologic disability, digit/limb amputation and skin scarring. You should provide 3rd generation cephalosporins along with supportive management.

stem: The culture you sent came back and suggests Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA). What is the best treatment option for this patient?
answer: The correct answer is D. MRSA infections can be treated with IV vancomycin. Note that vancomycin must be given IV as it is not well absorbed orally. Given how unwell this patient is, choosing an IV antibiotic is appropriate. All 3 other antibiotics have MSSA coverage but not MRSA.

stem: Alice is a 35-year-old female coming to the ED following an event in which she fell suddenly and lost consciousness. This event was unwitnessed. Alice is unable to recall how long she was unconscious for and cannot recall anything that happened during the event. She describes walking back to her car following a yoga class when she started to feel a bit “off”. Before she knew it, she was waking up on the pavement feeling a bit groggy and disoriented. She has been living with type 1 diabetes since age 11. She takes insulin and her sugars have been well controlled for many years. She does not take any other medications. She has no significant neurological history and has never experienced an event like this before. On the physical exam, she appears pale and fatigued. All vitals are within normal range with no orthostatics changes. Heart and lung sounds are normal. No abnormal findings are noted on the neurological exam. What are your top differential diagnoses at this time? Select up to 3 answers.
answer: The correct answer is A, B, C. It’s less likely to be hyperventilation since she didn’t describe feeling anxious or breathing heavily prior; less likely to be a TIA due to the abrupt episode; less likely to be a migraine as she didn’t describe experiencing any headache or visual disturbances; less likely to be a syncope with cardiac causes because she didn’t experience any angina or palpitation prior and there are no significant cardiovascular risk factors.

stem: Mr. Jenning is a 78-year-old man who presents to the emergency department after a fall in his retirement home. He has a history of hypertension, vascular dementia, Type 2 diabetes, osteoarthritis, chronic low back pain, atrial fibrillation, benign prostatic hypertrophy, bladder outlet obstruction, and COPD. He also had a transient ischemic attack five years ago. His daughter is present at the bedside and says that on several occasions in the last few days Mr. Jenning “had not been himself”. He had rambling speech, appeared to be confused, and asked her the same questions repeatedly. His daughter also notes that in the last year her father had several episodes of “confusion” involving word-finding difficulty and slurred speech. Which of the following of his medications are MOST LIKELY to have caused his fall? Select up to 5 answers.
answer: F, H, K, L, M. Glyburid is an SU used for his T2DM with higher risk of hypoglycemia. Terazosin is an alpha blocker for his BPH that could contribute to fall risk. Tramadol is an opioids likely used for his back pain, contributing to sedation, orthostatic hypotension and dizziness as fall risks. Both Ipratropium and Dimenhydrinate are anticholinergics, increasing the fall risk.

stem: During his course in hospital, Mr. Jenning becomes increasingly more confused and agitated. Which of the following additions to his assessment and history would be in keeping with behavioral and psychological symptoms of dementia as opposed to delirium? Select 2 answers.

options.html: Patient is taking temazepam for sleep
Patient appears sad, tearful, anxious, and irritable
Collateral history from his daughter suggesting that he has appeared increasingly more withdrawn over the past three months
Patient appears inattentive, and his responses do not make sense.
Patient has been experiencing visual hallucinations
Patient has experienced prior episodes of delirium Use this stem for questions 7-10: Mr. Johnson is a 75 year old man who was recently admitted for a COPD exacerbation with underlying pneumonia.

answer: The correct answer is B, C. It’s important to recognize that delirium is a fluctuation in mental status with a sudden onset, while symptoms of dementia or depression are developed slowly over months to years.

stem: During morning rounds, you check in with Mr. Johnson. He describes feeling unwell with right upper quadrant pain, and seems confused. You manage to learn from his wife that a bumbling incompetent clerk came in two nights ago and gave her husband a handful of pills that all looked the same. The clerk left the next morning without checking on Mr. Johnson and is not responding to text messages. You draw some bloodwork, which reveals the following: Hb – 121 g/dL (115-155 g/dL) WBCs – 5 (4-10) Platelets – 249 x 109/L (130-380 x 109/L) Na – 138 mmol/L (135-145 mmol/L) K – 4.0 mmol/L (3.5-5.1 mmol/L) Serum creatinine – 74 umol/L (22-75 umol/L) ALT – 3444 U/L (7-55 U/L) AST – 2991 U/L (8-48 U/L) GGT – 44 U/L (8-61 U/L) ALP – 87 U/L (45-115 U/L) Albumin – 20 g/dL (35-45 g/dL) Serum total bilirubin – 55 (<17) INR – 6.4 (0.9-1.2) TSH – 3.0 (0.4-5.5) Free T4 – 16 (9-23) Glucose – 5.2 mmol/L (4.0-7.0 mmol/L) From Mr. Johnson’s medication list, identify the most likely diagnosis and medication that the clerk gave to Mr. Johnson that could be responsible for these findings.
answer: Diagnosis - acute liver failure; medication - acetaminophen (most common cause of acute liver failure)

stem: Ms. Lahey is an 85 year old woman presenting to the emergency room with left lower abdominal pain. She tells you that the pain began as a dull achy feeling across her entire abdomen but can now point to the pain, in her left lower quadrant. Her only surgical history is that she had her gallbladder out in 1979. With this limited history, name 3 differential diagnoses for her pain.
answer: Diverticulitis, constipation, bowel obstruction, infectious colitis, ischemic colitis, inflammatory bowel disease (bimodal age distribution, possible to be diagnosed in older ages), (ruptured) ovarian cyst, ovarian torsion, uterine fibroid, hernia, renal stones/colic, UTI; likely many others! Bad guesses - appendicitis (wrong side), ectopic pregnancy (postmenopausal)

stem: Before you can ask any more questions, Ms. Lahey suddenly feels something wet. After returning from the bathroom, she tells you that there was a lot of blood in the toilet. It was bright red and it did not hurt. You ask about cancer screening, and she tells you she did her last FIT at age 74, after which she was told she no longer required screening. She does not have a family history of colorectal cancer. You ask her about her diet, and she tells you it consists mostly of trailer park food: hot dogs, cheeseburgers, and scalloped potatoes. She is not physically active. Her current medications include atorvastatin, ramipril, aspirin, and ibuprofen. Name 2 causes of rectal bleeding, and identify the most likely cause given her presentation with left lower abdominal quadrant pain.
answer: Diverticulitis - most common cause of massive, painless, bright red rectal bleeding, and her pain, age, poor diet, and lack of physical activity support this diagnosis; others - angiodysplasia, hemorrhoids, ischemic colitis, inflammatory bowel disease, infectious colitis, colorectal cancer, post-polypectomy; likely others! Bad guesses - any cause of upper GI bleeding (would have melena)
